div.p: Pneumosinus dilatans (PSD) is an abnormal expansion of the paranasal sinus beyond the normal anatomical boundaries of the sinus and the associated bone, with normal thickness of the sinus wall. It is a rare clinical condition, with a relatively small number of cases documented in the literature. Numerous theories have been proposed to explain the etiology of PSD, of which only the ball valve mechanism and Genetic predisposition with hormonal trigger have some scientific evidence. Usually detected incidentally by imaging, however, it may present with symptoms such as swelling of the forehead (with involvement of the frontal sinus), headache, nasal block, and symptoms related to mass effect on adjacent structures.

Imaging plays a major role in diagnosis, differential diagnosis, and identification of associated conditions, which is described in detail in this case report. The differential diagnosis includes hypersinus, pneumosinus, mucolcele, and benign sinus tumors. Conservative management by endoscopy is considered in asymptomatic patients, and surgical management is considered in patients with aesthetic concerns. We present a case of PSD in a 35-yearold female patient who presented with right-sided nasal obstruction and intermittent dull, nonradiating frontal headache for 3 years.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Pneumosinus dilatans (PSD) is an abnormal expansion of the paranasal sinus beyond the normal anatomical boundaries of the sinus with normal thickness of the sinus wall [ 1 ]. Due to rarity and unclear etiology, the condition is often under-recognised and detected incidentally on imaging done for symptoms such as headache or nasal block [ 2 ,3 ].

Numerous theories have been proposed to explain the etiology of PSD, of which only the ball valve mechanism and genetic predisposition with hormonal trigger have some scientific evidence [ 3 ,4 ]. Imaging plays a major role in diagnosis, differential diagnosis, identification of associated conditions, and guiding management [ 1 ,3 ,4 ,10 ]. We present a case of PSD in a middle-aged female patient with well-described imaging findings with supporting etiology of the ball valve mechanism. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.radcr.2025.12.

div.head: Case report
div.p: A 35-year-old female patient presented to the Department of Otorhinolaryngology with complaints of progressive rightsided nasal obstruction and intermittent dull, nonradiating frontal headache for 3 years. There was no associated epistaxis, visual disturbances, diplopia, or seizure. Clinical examination revealed mild mucosal congestion on the right side, without purulent discharge and a visible mass. There was no external facial deformity seen. No other significant past medical and family history. Based on the symptoms and clinical findings, chronic rhinosinusitis and frontal sinus mucocele were considered in the differential diagnosis. The patient was referred to the Department of Radiology for noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the paranasal sinuses (PNS). The CT PNS on the bone window revealed an enlarged right frontal sinus with bowing of the posterior wall, posteriorly and superiorly towards the anterior cranial fossa; however, normal thickness of the sinus wall was maintained ( Fig. 1 A and B). Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, along with the PNS, was performed to identify the associated conditions. MRI of the brain on T2-weighted imaging revealed an enlarged right frontal sinus with bowing of the posterior wall, causing a mild mass effect on the right frontal lobe; however, there was no obvious edema in the frontal lobe. Mild mucosal thickening was observed involving the right frontal sinus with a small polyp. There was also associated right ethmoidal and bilateral maxillary sinusitis ( Fig. 2 A, B, and C). The above findings are suggestive of frontal pneumosinus dilatans. No obvious associated meningiomas, arachnoid cysts, or fibrous dysplasia were observed by imaging. Routine blood investigations, biochemical parameters related to bone metabolism, and hormonal profile were within normal limits. Ball valve mechanism can be considered as a possible etiology, which is supported by the presence of a polyp in the sinus and the middle age of the patient. Genetic predisposition with hormonal trigger etiology is less likely, as it typically presents at a younger age, and there was no evidence of metabolic and hormonal abnormalities identified. The patient was advised of clinical follow-up and further surgical planning. However, the patent was subsequently lost to follow up.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: PSD is described as the abnormal expansion of single or multiple paranasal sinuses beyond the normal anatomical boundaries of both the sinus and the affected bone, with normal thickness of the sinus walls. The above condition should be differentiated from a hypersinus and pneumocele. Hypersinus is described as an expansion of the sinus beyond the normal anatomical boundaries of the sinus; however, it lies within the normal range of the affected bone with normal sinus wall thickness. Pneumocele is described as an expansion of the sinus beyond the anatomical boundaries with thinning of the bony sinus walls [1] . PSD is a rare condition, with a total of 171 cases documented in the literature [ 2 ]. Involvement of a single sinus is more common (84%) than that of multiple sinuses. In the single sinus, the frontal sinus is most involved (63%), followed by the sphenoid, maxillary, and ethmoid sinuses. PSD has a bimodal age distribution in the younger population (16-25 years) and the older population (36-45 years), and is more common in males. Most affected patients are young males in their third decade of life [ 3 ]. In this case report, the affected patient is female, which is uncommon.

Many theories have been proposed in the literature to describe the etiology, including the ball valve mechanism, fibro- osseous pathology, spontaneous drainage of mucocele, gasforming bacteria, hormonal disregulation, and genetic predisposition with a hormonal trigger; however, many of these theories lack sufficient scientific evidence. The ball valve mechanism in the older age group (36-45 years) and genetic predisposition with hormonal trigger in the younger age group (16-25 years) provide scientific evidence to explain the etiology of PSD. The ball valve mechanism is the most widely accepted theory, in which air is trapped in the sinus by a ball valve mechanism caused by an obstructive lesion (polyp, inflamed mucosa, or tumour). The genetic predisposition with hormonal trigger is proposed based on evidence of the rapid onset of symptoms with puberty, and an imbalance in sex hormones may play a role. The other theories do not have adequate scientific evidence [ 3 ,4 ]. PSD may be associated meningioma, arachnoid cysts, and fibrous dysplasia [ 2 ,5-7 ]. This case report demonstrates image evidence supporting the ball valve mechanism with identification of a frontal sinus polyp.

Most patients are asymptomatic; however, if they present with symptoms, their symptoms depend on the involved sinus, the structures displaced, and the associated lesions. Frontal sinus PSD most commonly presents with swelling over the forehead, a "Cro-Magnon-like" brow, which is of cosmetic concern. Other symptoms of PSD include headache, nasal blockage, facial deformity, diplopia, proptosis, exophthalmos, and impaired visual acuity. Ocular symptoms are most commonly and more severely associated with sphenoid and ethmoid sinus involvement or association with meningiomas, likely optic sheath meningioma [ 2 ,3 ,5 ].

Owing to the etiological enigma of PSD, a standardized approach is essential for clinical evaluation, surgical and nonsurgical management, and pathological analysis of PSD to elucidate its etiology [ 3 ]. Radiological evaluation via computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a pivotal role in evaluating the sinus involved, the number of sinuses involved, differentiating between the hypersinus and pneumocele, determining the mass effect on adjacent structures, identifying the causative factors (obstructive lesions), and identifying associated conditions (meningiomas, arachnoid cysts, fibrous dysplasia and chronic rhinosinusitis). CT is specifically used for the evaluation of bony abnormalities, and MRI has the advantage of superior soft tissue resolution and is used for the evaluation of associated conditions and evaluation of the mass effect on the brain and orbital components [ 2 ,3 ,8-10 ]. Blood samples are also collected for the assessment of abnormalities in bone metabolism and hormonal balance, which can help to determine an association with the theories of genetic predisposition with a hormone trigger or hormone dysregulation [ 3 ].

PSD should also be differentiated from other expansile sinus lesions such as hypersinus, pneumocele, mucocele, and benign sinus tumours. Mucocele shows soft tissue density on CT and variable signal intensity on MRI with sinus expansion and thinning or erosion of the sinus wall. Benign tumours show enhancing soft tissue masses with bony remodelling rather than uniform expansion [ 1 ,3 ,4 ,10 ].

If PSD is asymptomatic, detected incidentally, or has minimal frontal bossing, endoscopic widening of the frontal sinus ostium can be considered to relieve obstructive symptoms and to restore function. Most commonly, patients present with aesthetic concerns and rely on frontal bone reconstruction with open surgical procedures. The following surgical procedures are considered: The anterior wall of the frontal sinus was removed, inverted, and the resulting cavity was filled with bone dust from the donor site. The anterior wall of the frontal sinus was removed and replaced with small bones attached to a titanium mesh. The popular open surgical technique involves a bicoronal incision with the osteotomy and bone resurfacing of the outer table of the frontal bone [ 11 ].

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: PSD is a rare clinical condition with an enigma of etiopathogenesis, with only a few theories having supportive scientific evidence. Imaging plays a pivotal role in diagnosis, differential diagnosis, identification of etiological factors, identification of associated conditions, identification of changes due to mass effect, and guidance in management. The conclusions of this report are supported by the characteristic imaging findings and radiological support for the etiology of the ball valve mechanism. The strength of this case report is the comprehensive radiological assessment, and it also adds diagnostic value of the combined CT and MRI evaluation in PSD. A major limitation is the loss of follow-up of the patient to treatment.

figure.figDesc: Fig. 1 -Plain CT of PNS with bone window (A) Coronal section, (B) Axial section shows enlarged right frontal sinus (white arrow). Bowing of the posterior wall of the right frontal sinus, posteriorly and superiorly into the anterior cranial fossa, however, shows normal maintained thickness of the sinus wall (black arrow).

figure.head: Fig. 2 -
figure.figDesc: Fig. 2 -T2 weighted MRI of PNS (A) Coronal, (B) Sagittal, and (C) Axial sections show an enlarged right frontal sinus (white arrow) with mucosal thickening and showing small polyp (P). Posterior convexity of the posterior wall of the frontal sinus (black arrow) is causing mass effect seen on the adjacent frontal lobe (FL); however, shows no obvious oedema. Sinusitis of the right ethmoid sinus and bilateral maxillary sinuses is also noted (S).
